---
title: "Quiz: Bayesian image denoising"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Posterior energy $E(L) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}[L_p \ne L_q]$; with flip noise $\varepsilon$, a label that disagrees with the observed pixel costs $\log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$.

---

**Q1.** Where do the two terms of the posterior energy come from?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Bayes' rule, then $-\log$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$p(L \mid \mathbf y) \propto p(\mathbf y \mid L)\,p(L)$. The data term is $-\log$ of the likelihood (the noise model); the smoothness term is $-\log$ of the Ising prior (images have few disagreeing neighbours). $-\log$ turns the product into a sum.
:::

---

**Q2.** Flip noise with $\varepsilon = 0.01$ versus $\varepsilon = 0.3$: in which case does the data term weigh more, and why does that make sense?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compute $\log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\varepsilon = 0.01$: $\log 99 = 4.6$; $\varepsilon = 0.3$: $\log(7/3) = 0.85$. With rare flips an observed pixel is very likely right, so overriding it is expensive; with frequent flips the prior must do more of the work.
:::

---

**Q3.** What is the difference between the MAP and the MPM estimate? Which one makes fewer wrong pixels on average?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One decides the whole image jointly, the other each pixel separately.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
MAP: the single most probable image (lowest energy). MPM: for each pixel, its more probable value under the posterior marginal. The MPM minimises the expected number of wrong pixels; the MAP maximises the chance that the whole image is right.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does ICM get stuck, and why does annealing not?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What moves does each method allow?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
ICM only makes single-pixel changes that lower the energy, so it stops as soon as no single change helps: a local minimum (e.g. a small clump of noise pixels that support each other). Annealing samples at $T > 0$, which also accepts uphill moves; if cooled slowly it can leave such minima before $T$ gets low.
:::

---

**Q5.** How is the marginal $p(L_p = 1 \mid \mathbf y)$ obtained in practice, and what is it good for besides the MPM?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Unit 2.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Run a Gibbs sampler on the posterior at $T = 1$, discard the burn-in, and count the fraction of sweeps in which $L_p = 1$. It is an **uncertainty map**: values near 0.5 mark pixels the model cannot decide, typically along edges and in thin structures.
:::

---

**Q6.** For binary denoising, the exact MAP can be computed with one minimum cut. Why then compare ICM, annealing and mean field at all?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Think of other models, and of the MPM.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The cut works only for binary labels with $\lambda \ge 0$; for more labels or other priors the iterative methods are what is available. And the exact MAP is not always the best image: with a large $\lambda$ it removes thin structures that approximate methods (or the MPM) keep. The cut is the reference for judging optimisers, not the answer to every question.
:::

---

**Q7.** You increase $\lambda$. In which order do a disc of radius 20, a 3-pixel-wide line and a 1-pixel line disappear from the MAP?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Gain grows with area, cost with boundary length.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The 1-pixel line first (two boundaries per unit length against one pixel of data gain), then the 3-pixel line (two boundaries against three pixels), the disc last (its area grows faster than its perimeter). This is the shrinking bias of the graph-cut day.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* For flip noise in spin form, what is the field $h_p$ of the posterior Ising model?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$h_p = \tfrac12\log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\,y_p$: the observed spin, weighted by half the log-odds of a correct observation. $\log p(y_p \mid x_p) = \text{const} + h\,x_py_p$.
:::
